idiom_name: final monitor object over private state, with opaque types as unforgeable capabilities
implementation_notes: Scala supplies two things the classic structure needs. Private members are visible only to the class or trait itself and to its companion object (private[pkg] widens that to a package), so the monitor's policy and store can be unreachable from ordinary code. And opaque type aliases are transparent only inside their defining scope: the reference documentation's own example defines Permissions and PermissionChoice as opaque types whose only operations are extension methods, so code outside the object can neither forge a permission nor convert an Int into one - exactly the unforgeable capability a reference monitor hands out. The idiomatic realization is therefore an object with private state, one decide method, and grants represented as opaque capability values minted only by that object. As on any JVM language the compiler's visibility is not a security boundary: reflection, agents and --add-opens reach private members, so tamper resistance comes from the process or container boundary.
code_sketch:
object ReferenceMonitor:
  opaque type Capability = Long              // unforgeable outside this object
  private val store: PolicyStore = PolicyStore.empty

  def check(subject: Subject, action: Action, id: ObjectId): Option[Capability] =
    Option(subject.principal)                // no principal => None, fail closed
      .filter(p => store.allows(p, action, id))
      .map(_ => 1L)                          // minting is only possible in here

  def read(proof: Capability, id: ObjectId): Record =
    store.get(id)                            // callable only with a capability from check
pitfalls: private and private[pkg] are class- or package-scoped, not monitor-scoped: any code in the same package may reach the monitor's members, so the boundary has to be a package or module you control.

Opaque types erase to their underlying representation at runtime and are transparent inside the defining scope - a top-level opaque type is transparent throughout its file, so a helper in the same file can forge capabilities.

JVM reflection (setAccessible), instrumentation agents and --add-opens defeat Scala visibility exactly as they defeat Java's; treat the monitor as reviewable rather than tamperproof and put the enforcement boundary outside the JVM.

Implicit or given instances, and implicit conversions from the guarded type, let callers reach the policy store without passing the monitor; keep the store private and un-implicited and prefer explicit parameters in the monitor's API.
